title: Mechanisms and Machine Design
description: How linkages, cams, gears, shafts, bearings, springs and bolts make machines move, last and fit together.
audience: Adults who have done Engineering: Structures and Machines and want to see how real machines are put together. They know forces, moments, stress, simple gear ratios and levers, and basic trigonometry.
outcomes: You'll be able to count a mechanism's freedoms and judge a four-bar linkage.
You'll be able to size a spur-gear pair and read a planetary train.
You'll be able to estimate bearing life, spring rates and bolt preload.
You'll be able to read a tolerance fit and judge a fatigue risk.

modules.title: Linkages and cams
modules.summary: How a few rigid links and a profiled disc turn steady rotation into useful, controlled motion.

modules.title: Gears in depth

lessons.title: Counting what a mechanism can do
lessons.objective: Use the mobility formula to find how many inputs a planar linkage needs.

concepts.title: Links and joints
concepts.summary: A link is a rigid body; a joint is a connection that allows some relative motion and blocks the rest.

concepts.title: Mobility
concepts.summary: For a planar mechanism, M = 3(n - 1) - 2*j1 - j2, where n counts links including the fixed frame, j1 counts one-freedom joints and j2 counts two-freedom joints.

misconceptions: Learners count the frame as a link only sometimes, so every answer is off by three. The frame is a link because it is the reference body.
Learners think a mechanism with mobility 1 is weak or slow. Mobility 1 means one input fully decides the motion, which is what a machine wants.
A pin joint is counted as two joints when two links meet there. A pin joint joining two links is one joint; a pin through three links counts as two.
sequence: Start with a free body in a plane: three freedoms (x, y, turn).
Pin two bodies together and count what is lost: two freedoms.
Build the formula from that bookkeeping: each extra link adds 3, each pin takes away 2.
Apply to a triangle (mobility 0, a structure), a four-bar (1) and a five-bar (2).
Note the formula's limits: parallel links in special geometry can move although it says 0.
examples: Triangle of three links and three pins: n=3, j1=3, M=3*2-6=0, a rigid structure (ties back to trusses).
Five-bar: n=5, j1=5, M=3*4-10=2, so two motors are needed to place its coupler point.
Cam with a flat-faced follower sliding in a guide: frame, cam, follower; revolute cam-frame, prismatic follower-frame (j1=2), cam-follower contact (j2=1): M=3*2-4-1=1.

figures.shows: Four sketches (triangle, four-bar, five-bar, cam and follower) with links numbered and joints marked.
figures.learnerAction: Tap each joint to mark it counted; a tally of n, j1 and j2 fills in under the sketch.

figures.shows: The same four-bar drawn with one link highlighted as the fixed frame, then re-labelled with the frame hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the frame to see the count change.

historyNotes: Pafnuty Chebyshev (1850s) and Martin Grubler (1883) gave early versions of the mobility count; the planar form is usually named Grubler's or the Chebyshev-Grubler-Kutzbach criterion.

lessons.title: Four-bar linkages
lessons.objective: Say from four link lengths whether a four-bar can turn fully and where it transmits force badly.

concepts.title: Grashof condition
concepts.summary: If the shortest plus the longest link is no more than the sum of the other two, at least one link can rotate fully.

concepts.title: Transmission angle
concepts.summary: The angle between the coupler and the output link; near 90 degrees the coupler pushes the output efficiently, and below about 40 degrees the linkage jams or wears.

misconceptions: Learners expect the longest link to be the crank. The crank in a crank-rocker is the shortest link, next to the frame.
Learners think Grashof says the linkage works well. It says only that one link can turn fully, not that forces transmit well.
Learners confuse the transmission angle with the angle of any link to the horizontal; it is the angle between coupler and output, measured at their joint.
sequence: Name the four links: frame, crank, coupler, rocker.
Ask which link can make a full turn and show what blocks the others.
State the Grashof test s + l <= p + q and what it guarantees.
Classify: crank-rocker (shortest is the crank), double-crank (shortest is the frame), double-rocker (shortest is the coupler), non-Grashof triple-rocker.
Show a transmission angle sweeping through the stroke and where it is worst.
Window-wiper and sewing-machine needle as real crank-rockers.
examples: Links 20, 50, 40, 60 mm: s=20, l=60, s+l=80, p+q=90, so 80 <= 90 is Grashof. With the 20 mm link as the crank it is a crank-rocker.
Links 30, 40, 60, 80 mm: s+l=110, p+q=100, 110 > 100, not Grashof, so every link only rocks.
Links 30, 40, 60, 60 mm: s+l=90, p+q=100, Grashof by 10 mm of margin; the same four lengths with the 30 mm link as the frame give a double-crank.

figures.learnerAction: Drag the crank round; see the rocker swing and the transmission angle change.

figures.shows: Eight link-length sets with columns for s+l, p+q and Grashof yes/no hidden until the learner commits.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the yes/no for each set.

historyNotes: Franz Grashof (1826-1893) published the rotatability condition in his 1883 Theoretische Maschinenlehre.

lessons.title: Slider-cranks and quick returns
lessons.objective: Compute a slider-crank's stroke and position and explain how offset gives a quick return.

concepts.title: Stroke
concepts.summary: In a slider-crank with no offset the slider travels twice the crank radius.

concepts.title: Quick return
concepts.summary: When the forward and return strokes take different crank angles, the ratio of the longer to the shorter is the time ratio, (180 + a)/(180 - a) for offset angle a.

misconceptions: Learners expect the slider speed to be constant when the crank is. It slows to zero at each end of the stroke.
Learners think a longer connecting rod lengthens the stroke. Stroke is set by the crank radius only; the rod changes the shape of the motion.
Learners expect a quick-return machine to do more work per cycle. It only changes how the cycle is shared between cutting and returning.
sequence: Start from the engine: piston, rod, crank.
Write slider position x = r cos t + sqrt(l^2 - r^2 sin^2 t) and see the two extremes.
Stroke = 2r, independent of rod length.
Show speed going to zero at both ends and the piston's asymmetry for a short rod.
Offset the slider line so the forward and return sweeps are unequal angles.
Time ratio = (180 + a)/(180 - a); a shaper's cutting stroke runs slow, the return fast.
examples: Crank r=50 mm, rod l=200 mm: x(0)=250 mm, x(180)=150 mm, stroke 100 mm. At 90 degrees x=sqrt(200^2-50^2)=193.6 mm.
Offset angle a=30 degrees: time ratio (180+30)/(180-30)=210/150=1.4. At 60 rpm the working stroke takes 210/360 s = 0.583 s and the return 0.417 s.
Crank 20 mm gives a 40 mm stroke; with a 20 mm longer rod the stroke is unchanged.

figures.learnerAction: Drag the crank; shorten the rod and watch the curve lose symmetry.

figures.learnerAction: Set the offset; the forward and return arcs are shaded and their ratio shown after the learner estimates it.

lessons.title: Cams and followers
lessons.objective: Pick a cam motion law and find a follower's peak speed from rise, lift and angle.

concepts.title: Cam profile
concepts.summary: The cam's outline fixes the follower's displacement for every cam angle.

concepts.title: Motion law
concepts.summary: Constant velocity, simple harmonic and cycloidal motion trade peak speed and acceleration against smoothness.

misconceptions: Learners read the cam profile as the displacement graph. The graph is displacement against cam angle; the profile also depends on the base circle and follower.
Learners think constant-velocity motion is the gentlest. At its ends acceleration is theoretically infinite, which hammers the follower.
Learners assume bigger lift needs a bigger cam; the base circle sets size and pressure angle.
sequence: Build a displacement diagram: rise, dwell, return, dwell.
Constant velocity: simple slope, but corners.
Simple harmonic motion: s = (h/2)(1 - cos(pi t / T)), peak speed pi/2 times the average.
Cycloidal: smooth start and end, peak speed twice the average.
Pressure angle and base circle: why small cams jam.
Valve train as the standard example.
examples: Lift 20 mm in 0.25 s. Constant velocity: 80 mm/s. SHM peak: pi/2*80=125.7 mm/s. Cycloidal peak: 160 mm/s.
SHM peak acceleration pi^2 h/(2T^2)= pi^2*20/(2*0.0625)=1579 mm/s^2, about 1.58 m/s^2. Cycloidal: 2 pi h/T^2 = 2011 mm/s^2.
Cam turns at 60 rpm: 1 s per turn, so a 90-degree rise takes 0.25 s.

figures.shows: Displacement, velocity and acceleration curves for the three motion laws over one rise.
figures.learnerAction: Switch laws; drag the rise time and read peak values.

figures.shows: A disc cam, roller follower and its displacement diagram side by side.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the cam angle; a marker moves on both.

lessons.title: Why gear teeth are curved
lessons.objective: Compute pitch diameters, centre distance and module for a spur-gear pair and say why the involute is used.

concepts.title: Module
concepts.summary: Module m = pitch diameter / number of teeth in mm; two gears mesh only if their modules match.

concepts.title: Involute tooth
concepts.summary: An involute curve keeps the speed ratio constant even if the centre distance is slightly off, because contact stays on one fixed line of action.

concepts.title: Pressure angle
concepts.summary: The angle between the line of action and the common tangent of the pitch circles; 20 degrees is standard.

misconceptions: Learners think teeth of the same count mesh. They also need the same module and pressure angle.
Learners read the outside diameter as the pitch diameter; addendum adds 1 module each side, so da = m(z + 2).
Learners think the involute shape is chosen for looks; its geometry gives constant ratio and tolerance to centre-distance error.
sequence: Recall ratio from tooth counts (from the earlier gear-train lesson, not repeated).
Why a ratio from rolling cylinders would slip, and what teeth add.
Module and pitch circle: d = m z.
Centre distance a = m(z1 + z2)/2.
Involute: unwrap string from a base circle; base diameter db = d cos(phi).
Contact ratio above 1 so there is always a tooth in contact; undercut below about 17 teeth at 20 degrees.
examples: m=2 mm, z1=20, z2=45: d1=40, d2=90, centre distance 65 mm, ratio 2.25. Base circle of the small gear: 40*cos20=37.59 mm.
Outside diameter 124 mm, 60 teeth: m = 124/(60+2) = 2 mm.
Circular pitch p = pi*m = 6.283 mm for m=2.

figures.shows: gears model with driver 20, driven 45, input speed 1000 rpm; second case 20 and 30.
figures.learnerAction: Change tooth counts and see the speed and torque.

figures.shows: An involute drawn by unwrapping a string from a base circle, with the line of action and pressure angle marked.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the unwrapping point.

lessons.title: Planetary and worm gears
lessons.objective: Find the ratio of a planetary set and the lead angle that makes a worm drive self-locking.

concepts.title: Epicyclic train
concepts.summary: A sun, planets on a carrier and a ring share an axis, so a large ratio fits in a small volume.

concepts.title: Worm drive
concepts.summary: A worm of N starts drives a wheel of Z teeth with ratio Z/N, and may lock if friction beats the lead angle.

misconceptions: Learners treat the planets as idlers and ignore the carrier. The carrier carries the output.
Learners think planet size changes the ratio; it only sets ring size (Zr = Zs + 2Zp).
Learners think every worm is self-locking; it depends on the lead angle and friction.
sequence: Why a single stage stops at about 6:1 to 10:1 in practice.
Three parts on one axis; hold one, drive one, take the third.
Ring fixed, sun input, carrier output: ratio 1 + Zr/Zs.
Sun fixed, ring in, carrier out: 1 + Zs/Zr.
Worm: ratio Z/N; lead angle tan l = lead/(pi d); self-lock if l < friction angle.
Where each is used: automatic gearboxes, hub gears, steering, hoists.
examples: Sun 20, ring 80: planets (80-20)/2=30 teeth; ratio 1+80/20=5; sun at 1000 rpm gives carrier 200 rpm.
Sun fixed, ring 80 input: carrier at ring speed /(1+20/80)=0.8 of ring speed.
Worm single start, axial pitch 5 mm, pitch diameter 20 mm: tan l = 5/(pi*20)=0.0796, l=4.55 degrees; wheel of 40 teeth gives 40:1.

figures.shows: Planetary set with sun, three planets, carrier and ring; each part can be set as fixed, input or output.
figures.learnerAction: Choose roles and read the ratio; a locked part highlights.

figures.shows: gears model with two stages, 20/60 then 15/45.
figures.learnerAction: Compare with the single planetary stage.

lessons.title: What gears push on, and what shafts carry
lessons.objective: Resolve a gear tooth force and find a shaft's torsion stress and twist.

concepts.title: Tooth force
concepts.summary: The tooth force is normal to the tooth; its tangential part carries the torque, its radial part pushes the gears apart.

concepts.title: Torsion
concepts.summary: A solid round shaft carrying torque T has surface shear stress 16T/(pi d^3) and twists by TL/(GJ).

misconceptions: Learners treat the torque as the force. The tangential force is torque divided by pitch radius.
Learners forget the radial component, which loads the bearings.
Learners think doubling the diameter doubles shaft strength. It multiplies it by eight.
sequence: Tangential force Ft = T/r.
Radial force Fr = Ft tan(phi), normal force Ft/cos(phi).
These become shaft bending and bearing loads.
Torque from power: T = P/w.
Shear stress and twist in a solid round shaft; d^3 and d^4.
Stress concentrations at keyways and shoulders.
examples: Torque 40 N*m, pitch radius 50 mm: Ft=800 N, Fr=800*tan20=291.2 N, normal 851.3 N.
5 kW at 1500 rpm: w=157.08 rad/s, T=31.83 N*m. A 20 mm steel shaft: tau=20.3 MPa.
Twist over 0.5 m with G=80 GPa: 0.73 degrees.

figures.shows: gears model, 20/45, input torque 40 N*m, with arrows on the tooth contact.
figures.learnerAction: Change torque and see how the shaft torque scales by the ratio.

figures.shows: Shaft cross-section with shear stress shown growing linearly from the axis outward.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the diameter; stress falls as d cubed.

lessons.title: Bearings and how long they last
lessons.objective: Estimate rolling-bearing life from load and rating, and choose plain or rolling.

concepts.title: L10 life
concepts.summary: The number of million revolutions that 90 percent of identical bearings survive: L10 = (C/P)^p.

concepts.title: Bearing types
concepts.summary: Plain bearings run on a lubricant film and suit high load at low speed; rolling bearings trade a small start-up friction for rolling contact.

misconceptions: Learners treat L10 as the life of each bearing. 10 percent fail earlier and half last about five times longer.
Learners expect life to fall in proportion to load; for ball bearings it falls with the cube.
Learners think rolling beats plain in every case; a plain bearing tolerates shock and is quieter and cheaper.
sequence: Why friction and wear decide bearing design.
Plain bearing and the oil film; rolling: balls and rollers.
Dynamic rating C: load for 1 million revolutions.
L10 = (C/P)^3 for balls, ^(10/3) for rollers.
Preload, clearance and lubrication, briefly.
examples: C=14 kN, P=2 kN, ball: L10 = 7^3 = 343 million revolutions. At 1500 rpm: 343e6/(60*1500)= 3811 h.
Same loads with roller bearings: 7^(10/3) = 656 million revolutions.
Doubling P cuts a ball bearing's life to 1/8.

figures.learnerAction: Move the load; the point slides along each curve.

figures.learnerAction: Tap parts to label inner race, outer race, cage.

lessons.title: Springs
lessons.objective: Find a helical spring's stiffness, stress and natural frequency, and combine springs.

concepts.title: Spring rate
concepts.summary: k = G d^4 /(8 D^3 N) for a helical compression spring with wire diameter d, mean coil diameter D and N active coils.

concepts.title: Wahl factor
concepts.summary: The shear stress in the wire is raised by a curvature factor Kw = (4C-1)/(4C-4) + 0.615/C, where C = D/d.

misconceptions: Learners think the wire is loaded in tension. A helical spring twists the wire.
Learners add stiffnesses of springs in series. In series, flexibilities add.
Learners think thicker coils make a stiffer spring, but D enters as D cubed in the denominator.
sequence: Springs store energy: E = 1/2 k x^2.
Twist the wire: the coil is a torsion bar wrapped round.
Series and parallel combinations.
Stress: tau = Kw 8FD/(pi d^3).
Spring plus mass gives natural frequency f = sqrt(k/m)/2pi; surge in fast machines.
examples: Two 4 N/mm springs in series: 2 N/mm; in parallel 8 N/mm.
Mass 0.5 kg on k=3906 N/m: f=14.1 Hz.

lessons.title: Bolted joints and preload
lessons.objective: Find tightening torque and the share of an external load a bolt carries.

concepts.title: Preload
concepts.summary: A bolt works as a stiff spring pulling parts together; the initial tension is preload.

concepts.title: Joint constant
concepts.summary: C = kb/(kb+km) is the share of an added load that the bolt carries; the rest relieves clamping.

misconceptions: Learners think the bolt carries the whole external load. Usually it carries a small share, because the clamped parts are much stiffer.
Learners think tighter is always better; preload is set below proof strength.
Learners read a bolt as a rigid pin rather than a spring.
sequence: Why joints use friction, not shear, in many designs.
Bolt and clamped parts as two springs.
Preload target: about 75 percent of proof load.
Torque T = K F d.
Load share: bolt rise = C P; clamp loss = (1-C) P.
Separation at P = Fi/(1-C); property class 8.8 means 800 MPa tensile, 640 MPa yield.
examples: M10x1.5, stress area 58 mm^2, class 8.8 proof 580 MPa: 75 percent preload = 0.75*580*58 = 25.2 kN.
T = 0.2*20000*0.01 = 40 N*m for a 20 kN preload.
kb:km = 1:4, so C=0.2; external 10 kN raises the bolt by 2 kN and clamping falls by 8 kN. Separation at 20/0.8 = 25 kN.

figures.learnerAction: Drag the load; the bolt and clamp shares update.

figures.shows: Cutaway bolt joint showing thread, clamped plates and the load path.
figures.learnerAction: Hover to see friction vs shear.

lessons.title: Fits and tolerances
lessons.objective: Read an ISO fit code and compute clearance or interference.

concepts.title: Fit
concepts.summary: The relationship between a shaft and a hole: clearance, transition or interference.

concepts.title: Basic-hole system
concepts.summary: The hole is fixed with zero lower deviation (H); fits vary by shaft deviation letters.

misconceptions: Learners read a tolerance as an error. It is permission to vary.
Learners expect smaller tolerances always better; they cost more.
Learners add stack-up tolerances linearly always; statistical stack-up combines them as the root of the sum of squares.
sequence: Why no part is exactly its nominal size.
Tolerance grades (IT6, IT7) and deviation letters.
Hole H7 for 25 mm: 0 to +21 micrometres.
Shaft g6: -20 to -7 micrometres; p6: +22 to +35.
Clearance and interference from the extremes.
Stack-up: worst case vs root-sum-square.
examples: 25 H7/p6: shaft 25.022-25.035; interference 0.001 to 0.035 mm.
Three parts each +/-0.10: worst case +/-0.30, RSS sqrt(3*0.01)=0.173.

lessons.title: How parts fail
lessons.objective: Use Goodman and Miner to judge fatigue safety, and name the other common failure modes.

concepts.title: Fatigue
concepts.summary: Repeated stress far below yield can grow a crack until the part breaks.

concepts.title: Goodman line
concepts.summary: sa/Se + sm/Su = 1/n combines alternating and mean stress into a safety factor.

misconceptions: Learners think a part that survives the first load survives forever.
Learners think strength alone fixes life; surface finish and notches matter.
Learners add the stress concentration factor to stress; it multiplies.
sequence: Static failure: yield, fracture, buckling.
The S-N curve and the endurance limit (about half of Su for steels).
Modifiers: finish, size, load.
Stress concentration Kt.
Goodman safety factor.
Miner's cumulative damage.
examples: Hole in plate: Kt about 3; 40 MPa nominal becomes 120 MPa.
10^5 cycles with N=4*10^5 (0.25) plus 2*10^5 with N=10^6 (0.2): damage 0.45.

figures.shows: S-N curve on log axes with the endurance limit as a knee.
figures.learnerAction: Move the stress; read the cycles.
